old: Use gustar, preferir, encantar and parecer to express reactions to cultural works. Opinion phrases such as *creo* *que*, me parece que and *para* mí allow you to distinguish a personal response from a neutral description.
new: You know *gustar* and *encantar* from A1 Unit 22, the stem-changing verb *preferir* from A1 Unit 8, and the opinion phrases *creo que* and *me parece que* from B1 Unit 13. Here you use them to react to films, books and music. *Para mí* introduces your own view and separates it from a neutral description.
why: screen presents A1/B1 forms as new: recap with the unit numbers

old: *Gustar*, *encantar* and *parecer* agree with the thing being reacted to, not with the person reacting — that's why it's *me* *encanta* *esta* *película* (singular film) but *me* *encantan* *estas* *películas* (plural films), never *encanto*.
new: *Encantar* agrees with the thing you like, not with you: *Me encanta esta película* (one film) but *Me encantan estas películas* (several films).
why: garbled tip with one italic run per word

old: Evaluation combines descriptive language with judgements. Expressions such as es *interesante*, está *bien* hecha, *resulta* *convincente* and no me *parece* original allow you to assess a work. When giving a reason, connect the judgement to a specific feature such as the plot, characters or performance.
new: You know *me parece que* from B1 Unit 13. New here: *resultar* + adjective gives a judgement about a work and means \"to come across as\" or \"to turn out to be\". The adjective agrees with the thing you judge: *El argumento resulta convincente*, *Los personajes resultan convincentes*. Connect every judgement to a feature such as the plot, the characters or the performance.
why: the lesson's own skill (resultar + adjective) was never explained; recap of parecer added

old: An evaluation should give a judgement and a reason, rather than only saying that something is good or bad.
new: *Resultar* is used with the same adjectives as *ser*, but it sounds like a considered judgement: *El final resulta previsible porque ya conocemos la historia.*
why: tip did not teach the skill; replaced by one natural sentence

old: Recommendations commonly use recomendar *que*, aconsejar que and ser *importante* que followed by the subjunctive. The recommendation can also be expressed directly with deberías or te *recomiendo* que. At B1, focus on the common pattern: recommendation + que + subjunctive.
new: You know *te recomiendo que* + subjunctive from B1 Unit 7 and *es importante que* + subjunctive from A2 Unit 27. Here you use them to recommend films, books and music: *recomendar que*, *aconsejar que* and *es importante que* are followed by the present subjunctive (*veas*, *escuches*, *leas*), and so is *merecer que*.
why: screen presents B1 Unit 7 / A2 Unit 27 material as new: recap

old: After a recommendation with *que*, use the present subjunctive when the person recommended to do the action is different from the person making the recommendation.
new: The person who recommends and the person who acts are different: *Yo te recomiendo que tú leas esta novela.* If you say what you yourself will do, use the infinitive: *Voy a leer esta novela.*
why: tip garbled/vague: one natural pair showing the point

old: Compare cultural works with *más*/menos... *que* and tan... como. Relative clauses with que and donde identify people, works and places without repeating information. These structures are useful when explaining similarities and differences.
new: You know *más … que* and *tan … como* from A2 Unit 6, and relative clauses with *que* and *donde* from B1 Unit 9. Here you use them together: you compare two works, and a relative clause tells the reader which work you mean or adds a fact about it.
why: screen presents A2 Unit 6 and B1 Unit 9 forms as new: recap
